title: Sauteed Spicy Sukuma Wiki
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Collard greens folded into ginger, onion, tomato and chilli oil and cooked just five to seven minutes, until they turn bright green and still have a crunch.
longDesc: Sukuma wiki means to push the week — collard greens are what stretches a household through to the next payday, and the plant is a survivor that comes back green after months of drought and a week of rain. The cooking is fast and the cue is colour: bright green, five to seven minutes, still with a crunchy raw feel if you like it that way. If the tomatoes make it too sour, a sprinkle of sugar is the fix, and that is a real Ugandan kitchen habit rather than a modern adjustment.
ingredients: 2 or more bunches sukuma wiki (collard greens), thinly cut
Thinly sliced onion, crushed nuts or simsim
steps: Thinly cut the sukuma wiki and set it aside.
Put a pan on high heat with oil and let it get hot.
Add the ginger and onions and let them fry until almost golden.
Add the tomatoes, chilli oil and salt and stir. Let the tomatoes cook until tender.
Add the sukuma wiki and fold it in well.
Let it cook 5 to 7 minutes, or until it turns a bright green colour.
Garnish with thinly sliced onion and crushed nuts or simsim, and serve with posho.
chefTips: Bright green is the doneness cue. Past that you get the grey, collapsed greens nobody wants.
Five to seven minutes. If you want it more tender, cook it a little longer — but the crunchy raw feel is the preferred texture.
Tomatoes add a tangy sourness. To reduce it, sprinkle in some sugar. That is the standard fix and it works.
Cut the greens thin. Thick ribbons need longer than the tomatoes can wait.
Fold them in rather than stirring hard. You want them coated, not bruised.
Sukuma wiki is mostly served alongside posho, and any East African will tell you the same.
Crushed nuts or simsim on top is not decoration — it adds the protein and fat the dish otherwise lacks.
commonMistakes: Adding them before the tomatoes are tender.
Ignoring the sourness rather than adding a little sugar.
Stirring hard enough to break them up.
sources: Adapted from Sophia Musoki, 'Sauteed Spicy Sukuma Wiki', A Kitchen In Uganda (11 August 2016) — the ingredient list, the method and the bright-green doneness cue with its 5-to-7-minute window are hers.

Her observations are reproduced closely: she prefers the sukuma wiki to still have a crunchy raw feel and says to cook it longer if you want it more tender; tomatoes add a tangy sour taste and sprinkling in some sugar reduces it; and sukuma wiki is mostly served alongside posho.

The translation of sukuma wiki as to push the week, and her note that the plant survives months of sun and greens up after a week of rain, are from the same post. That source gives no weights for the greens or the oil.
reheating: Warm briefly — it will lose the crunch.
healthBenefits: Collard greens are very high in vitamins K, A and C, plus calcium and folate.
Short cooking preserves far more of the vitamin C than a long braise.
Simsim or nuts on top add calcium, protein and healthy fats.
Low in calories and high in fibre.
culturalNote: The name is the whole story — sukuma wiki pushes the week, because it is cheap, it grows fast and it keeps coming back. It is the most-eaten green in East Africa for exactly that reason, and it is served with posho so consistently that the pairing is almost a single dish.
